Fast-Growth & Fundraising
The ambitious UK companies raising venture capital

Introduction
As one of the most common types of investors 
deploying equity ﬁnance in the UK, private equity 
and venture capital funds are a central part of the 
country’s high-growth ecosystem.
 
Whilst the amount of capital available in the UK’s 
startup landscape continues to grow, our research 
has indicated that this is increasingly being 
deployed to later-stage businesses, with 
early-stage startups being left out in the cold. 
So what do the companies that managed to secure 
their ﬁrst round of funding from a private equity or 
venture capital ﬁrm in 2021 have in common? 
In this report, we explore these ambitious 
businesses’ growth journeys, to get a picture of 
what it takes to secure venture ﬁnance in the UK 
right now. Using these commonalities as indicators, 
we then spotlight four startups likely to be seeking 
capital from private equity or VC ﬁrms in 2022.

First-time VC rounds in 2021
Between January and November 2021, an impressive 552 UK 
companies announced their ﬁrst private equity or venture 
capital funding round. 
Deal numbers remained relatively steady throughout the 
year but peaked dramatically in March, at 124 ﬁrst-time 
PE/VC rounds, compared to an average of 45 deals in other 
months. This March spike is in keeping with wider trends 
across the UK funding landscape this year, particularly for 
deals involving PE/VC funds. 
Amount raised also peaked in March (£322m), perhaps a 
result of delayed investments from 2020, amidst COVID 
market hesitation. Despite dropping back down in Q2 and 
Q3, amount raised resurged somewhat in November, landing 
on £287m worth of ﬁrst-time PE/VC rounds for the month. 
Volume and value of ﬁrst-time PE/VC deals 
announced (Jan-Nov 2021)

Stage of evolution
When raising their ﬁrst round with a PE/VC fund this year, 
50% of investee companies were operating at the seed 
stage. This means they were young businesses, with a 
relatively low employee count and valuation, little to no 
investment secured, and an uncertain product-market ﬁt. 
Meanwhile, around a third (34%) were operating at the 
venture stage at the time of their ﬁrst PE/VC 
deal—companies with an established business model and 
revenue streams that have likely been around for several 
years, and may be expanding their initial product or service 
range. 
Given that PE/VC funds tend to invest in earlier-stage 
companies, it comes as no surprise to ﬁnd that seed and 
venture-stage startups were by far the most common 
recipients of ﬁrst-time venture funding.
Company stage of evolution at time of 
ﬁrst PE/VC-backed deal

Employee count
The vast majority of companies that secured their ﬁrst 
PE/VC round in 2021 (and for which employee count was 
known) had fewer than 25 employees at the time of 
fundraising, at 77%. A far smaller proportion had employee 
numbers of 25-50 (10%), 50-75 (5%) and 75-100 (2%). 
Only 23 companies are known to have had more than 100 
employees. Three businesses had more than 500 employees: 
healthcare ﬁrm PAM (543), social care provider CSN Care 
Group (1,133), and contact centre outsourcer ResQ (1,325). 
On the whole, companies with relatively few employees are 
more likely to need and be seeking equity investment, and 
were thus far more likely to secure ﬁrst-time PE/VC funding 
this year than their peers.
Employee count reported in ﬁlings prior to 
ﬁrst PE/VC investment

EBITDA
Of the 54 businesses that disclosed company ﬁnancials 
prior to their ﬁrst PE/VC fundraising, 78% reported positive 
earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and 
amortisation (EBITDA). Most businesses (91%) reported an 
EBITDA between -£1m and £6m. 
Just three companies exceeded this, with the maximum 
reported ﬁgure being £31.9m, by established supply chain 
management and transport logistics ﬁrm Ligentia. None of 
the businesses that received their ﬁrst round of PE/VC 
funding this year had an EBITDA of less than -£4m. 
Businesses with relatively small, positive EBITDA were most 
likely to secure investment from PE/VC funds, having proven 
some traction, with the potential to produce strong ROI for 
investors.
EBITDA reported in ﬁlings prior to ﬁrst 
PE/VC investment

Operating proﬁt
The operating proﬁt of businesses securing PE/VC funding 
for the ﬁrst time in 2021 follows a very similar trend to 
EBITDA ﬁgures: 74% of companies reported positive 
operating proﬁts prior to their PE/VC raise. 
Similarly to EBITDA, 91% of investee companies reported 
operating proﬁts between -£1m and £6m. The lowest 
reported proﬁts were -£3.85m, whilst Ligentia again marked 
the upper bound of the range, at £30.9m.
Businesses with relatively small but positive operating 
proﬁts are the most likely to secure PE/VC backing. 
Operating proﬁt reported in ﬁlings prior to 
ﬁrst PE/VC investment

Previous equity deals
Around half of investee companies already had equity 
fundraisings under their belt prior to their ﬁrst PE/VC round 
this year. But the remaining 270 businesses (49%) had never 
raised equity ﬁnance before.
One in four businesses (26%) had secured one previous 
equity deal ahead of their PE/VC round, whilst 11% had 
secured two. The more equity fundraisings a company had, 
the less likely they were to raise ﬁrst-time PE/VC funding in 
2021—just 4% had secured ﬁve or more rounds.  
Private equity and venture capital ﬁrms like to see a certain 
amount of traction before investing in a business. For 
businesses to gain this traction, they often require other 
forms of ﬁnance ﬁrst, such as loans, or angel and 
family/friend rounds. 
Number of equity rounds secured prior to ﬁrst 
PE/VC investment

Existing investors
Where the funds involved were disclosed, 46 of these 
previous equity deals saw participation from angel investors, 
including both individual angels (30) and networks (21). 
But crowdfunding platforms were the most common single 
source of funding, facilitating 35 rounds secured by 
businesses prior to their ﬁrst-time PE/VC raise in 2021. This 
method of fundraising for early-stage startups with an 
engaged customer base has become increasingly popular 
over the past decade. 
These ﬁgures show that early investors in high-growth 
companies are often individuals rather than institutions. But 
whilst angel investing and crowdfunding is used to develop 
a proof of concept or minimum viable product, ambitious 
businesses often need the investment of PE/VC funds to 
then reach the next stage in their growth journeys.
Fund types involved prior to ﬁrst 
PE/VC investment

Time since previous raise
Of those that had already secured equity investment, 37% 
had last done so in the 12 months before their ﬁrst PE/VC 
round. Meanwhile, the majority (78%) had raised their 
previous funding round up to two years prior.
Once a company has secured an initial round of funding, 
they will likely experience a sharp period of growth as they 
put that capital to work. Following this, they’ll then need and 
have the capacity to take on larger sums of money. 
Since businesses usually start preparing for a new 
fundraising at least six months in advance, those that last 
raised around 4-6 months ago may well be considering their 
ﬁrst PE/VC round.
Number of months since equity round prior to ﬁrst 
PE/VC investment

Value of previous rounds
Of the 275 companies that had secured previous equity 
rounds and the amount raised is known, 42% had secured 
less than £500k ahead of their ﬁrst PE/VC round this year. 
And the majority (62%) of businesses had raised less than 
£1m. 
An additional 31% has previously raised between £1m and 
£5m. Just 18 companies had raised more than £5m prior to 
securing their ﬁrst round of venture ﬁnance in 2021. 
Unsurprisingly, companies that have only small amounts of 
equity funding are far more likely to need growth capital 
than those with signiﬁcant investments under their belts. 
They’re thus more likely to seek investment from private 
equity ﬁrms or VCs.
Amount of equity investment secured prior to 
PE/VC investment

4 fast-growth 
companies likely to 
be fundraising soon

Key indicators
As expected, the types of companies most likely to 
be on the lookout for funding from private equity 
and venture capital ﬁrms are early-stage startups 
with relatively few (<25) employees, looking to 
scale their business. 
Our research also indicates they’re likely to have 
secured either no prior equity investment or less 
than £1m, through a small number of rounds (most 
likely involving angels or the crowd). If they have 
secured funding, then their most recent round will 
likely have occured four to six months ago.
Those reporting small but positive EBITDA and 
operating proﬁts will be in a better position to gain 
PE/VC backing than their peers. 
We’ve picked out four high-growth UK companies 
that match this proﬁle and are hence likely to be 
seeking venture ﬁnance in the near future. 
Last year, two of the businesses that we predicted 
would start fundraising soon (Supernotes and 
Deepﬁnity) did in fact raise new investment, within 
three months of our report being published.    
Fast-growth companies likely to be fundraising

1. Boxx
Boxx provides at-home and in-studio ﬁtness 
classes, specialising in boxing workouts. Founded 
in 2016 by Anna Samuels, the company is currently 
based in Redbridge, East London. 
Boxx attended Libra 1.0, Tech Nation’s accelerator 
programme for tech companies with at least one 
Black or multiracial founder, between September 
2021 and March 2022.
Boxx is likely to seek investment from private 
equity and venture capital ﬁrms soon, meeting
many of our key indicators: it’s currently operating 
at the seed stage, has 5-9 employees, and has 
secured just one equity fundraising so far. 
The £155k round took place in June 2021 (six 
months ago), at a post-money valuation of £1.57m. It 
saw involvement from Cornerstone Partners, an 
angel network that supports diverse founding 
teams in the UK, as well as individual angel 
investors.   
Fast-growth companies likely to be fundraising

2. Valentian Vermouth
Valentian Vermouth was founded in 2017, and is 
currently headquartered in Melrose, in the Scottish 
Borders. The drinks company has paired wines from 
small batch producers in Italy with a Scottish new 
make malt spirit, usually reserved for single malt 
whisky. 
It already stocks its range of vermouths in several 
bars in Scotland, and was awarded a £4k grant by 
the Scottish Borders Business Fund, back in 
February 2020. 
In June 2021 (six months ago), Valentian Vermouth 
secured its ﬁrst equity round, worth £111k, at a 
post-money valuation of £510k. The raise was 
facilitated by crowdfunding platform Crowdcube, 
and will be used to open Valentian Vermouth’s ﬁrst 
location, and hire a PR agency and in-house sales 
team. 
With just 1 employee as of March this year, we 
expect this seed-stage company will be seeking 
additional funding from VCs soon. 
Fast-growth companies likely to be fundraising

3. Skyfarer
Based in Coventry, Skyfarer is developing a system 
of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) for the delivery 
of medical supplies, such as blood and vaccines, at 
speed. Skyfarer’s low-cost system will enable 
companies, NGOs and governments to introduce 
drones to their logistics, from infrastructure 
development to humanitarian aid networks. 
Founded in mid-2019, it entered the European 
Space Agency Business Incubation Centre (ESA BIC 
UK) accelerator programme in August 2021. 
Skyfarer meets several of our criteria for 
companies likely to be seeking venture ﬁnance. The 
venture-stage startup has fewer than 25
employees, and just one equity fundraising under 
its belt. Having secured a £49.4k Innovate UK grant 
in July 2020 (as part of a six-month project), 
Skyfarer raised pre-seed investment from Minerva 
Business Angel Network in July 2021 (ﬁve months 
ago) to support its trials—although the amount 
raised was not disclosed. 
Conﬁrming our suspicions, according to Skyfarer’s 
LinkedIn page, the company is currently “looking 
for capital funding to develop our ﬁnal prototype 
and set up a robust operational process into an 
operational platform that can be scaled nationally“.
Fast-growth companies likely to be fundraising

4. Black Ballad
Founded in 2014, Black Ballad operates a lifestyle 
platform focused on the experiences of Black 
women in the UK, and provides an online 
publication for Black-owned brands and content. 
The London-based media company attended the 
King’s20 accelerator in September 2018, a one-year 
programme for startups led by students, staff or 
alumni of King’s College London. 
In February 2020, it also received a £70k grant to 
tell the stories of Black women outside of London, 
on their own terms. The grant was awarded by 
Future of News Fund, powered by NESTA and 
Bethnal Green Ventures.
More recently, Black Ballad secured its ﬁrst equity 
investment, a £337k crowdfunding round via 
Seedrs, in July 2021 (ﬁve months ago). The company 
is currently operating at the venture stage, and has 
between 10 and 24 employees. Based on these 
indicators, we think Black Ballad is likely to be 
seeking venture ﬁnance soon. 
Fast-growth companies likely to be fundraising

the Beauhurst platform, from early-stage startups 
to scaleups.

hundreds of users to ﬁnd, engage, and win exciting 
new business, in less time than ever before.

small batch producers in Italy with a Scottish new
make malt spirit, usually reserved for single malt
whisky.
It already stocks its range of vermouths in several
bars in Scotland, and was awarded a £4k grant by
the Scottish Borders Business Fund, back in
February 2020.

In June 2021 (six months ago), Valentian Vermouth
secured its first equity round, worth £111k, at a
post-money valuation of £510k. The raise was
facilitated by crowdfunding platform Crowdcube,
and will be used to open Valentian Vermouth’s first
location, and hire a PR agency and in-house sales
team.
With just 1 employee as of March this year, we
expect this seed-stage company will be seeking
additional funding from VCs soon.

Based in Coventry, Skyfarer is developing a system
of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) for the delivery
of medical supplies, such as blood and vaccines, at
speed. Skyfarer’s low-cost system will enable
companies, NGOs and governments to introduce
drones to their logistics, from infrastructure
development to humanitarian aid networks.
Founded in mid-2019, it entered the European
Space Agency Business Incubation Centre (ESA BIC
UK) accelerator programme in August 2021.
Skyfarer meets several of our criteria for
companies likely to be seeking venture finance. The
venture-stage startup has fewer than 25

employees, and just one equity fundraising under
its belt. Having secured a £49.4k Innovate UK grant
in July 2020 (as part of a six-month project),
Skyfarer raised pre-seed investment from Minerva
Business Angel Network in July 2021 (five months
ago) to support its trials—although the amount
raised was not disclosed.
Confirming our suspicions, according to Skyfarer’s
LinkedIn page, the company is currently “looking
for capital funding to develop our final prototype
and set up a robust operational process into an
operational platform that can be scaled nationally“.

Founded in 2014, Black Ballad operates a lifestyle
platform focused on the experiences of Black
women in the UK, and provides an online
publication for Black-owned brands and content.
The London-based media company attended the
King’s20 accelerator in September 2018, a one-year
programme for startups led by students, staff or
alumni of King’s College London.
In February 2020, it also received a £70k grant to
tell the stories of Black women outside of London,
on their own terms. The grant was awarded by

Future of News Fund, powered by NESTA and
Bethnal Green Ventures.
More recently, Black Ballad secured its first equity
investment, a £337k crowdfunding round via
Seedrs, in July 2021 (five months ago). The company
is currently operating at the venture stage, and has
between 10 and 24 employees. Based on these
indicators, we think Black Ballad is likely to be
seeking venture finance soon.
